name: Orbital decompression
lead: Orbital decompression is surgery that enlarges the effective volume of the eye socket by removing orbital bone, orbital fat, or both, allowing the eye to sit further back. Its established use is in thyroid eye disease (Graves' orbitopathy), where swollen muscle and fat push the eye forward (proptosis) and can compress the optic nerve.[9][10]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way for people without thyroid disease to get deeper-set eyes by reducing protrusion, and members debate who is a candidate, which technique (fat removal or bone work) is used, and its risks.[18][21]

The clinical literature on orbital decompression concerns people with thyroid eye disease. Randomised trials and case series compare surgical approaches and report outcomes such as proptosis reduction and sight-threatening optic neuropathy.[7][8][9] No published trial located assesses the procedure for purely cosmetic deep-setting in people with normal thyroid and orbital status, and the surgery is an operation in the orbit with documented risks to vision and eye movement.[9][5]

paras: Orbital decompression changes the volume relationship inside the bony eye socket. The orbit is a rigid cavity holding the eye, six muscles, nerves, vessels and fat; when contents swell or the socket is small, the eye is pushed forward. By taking away a wall of bone, some orbital fat, or both, a surgeon lets the contents shift back so the eye sits deeper in the socket.[10][28]

For appearance, the goal is a less prominent eye and a deeper-set look. In thyroid eye disease the operation is often described by clinicians as rehabilitative: it restores function and appearance once inflammation has settled.[29] Protrusion is measured with an exophthalmometer, and many sources treat a reading above about 18 mm as proptosis.[33]

The procedure belongs to a family of orbital and periocular operations that also includes eyelid retraction surgery, strabismus surgery, blepharoplasty and orbital fat grafting; in looksmaxxing language these fall under 'eye area hardmaxxing', and decompression is the one aimed at pushing the globe backward rather than adding or lifting tissue around it.[10][19]

Graves' orbitopathy, also called thyroid eye disease, is an autoimmune condition in which the orbital muscles and fat swell, producing proptosis, eyelid retraction, double vision and sometimes optic nerve compression. Irish surgeon Robert Graves described the link between thyroid enlargement and eye protrusion in 1835.[10]

Guidelines emphasise stage-adapted anti-inflammatory therapy, risk-factor control including smoking cessation, and rehabilitative surgery after inflammation stabilises. Compressive optic neuropathy is treated as an emergency.[1][3][5] Orbital decompression is used both urgently for optic neuropathy and electively to reduce proptosis.[10]

sections.h: Thyroid eye disease: the main patient population
paras: Most published decompression surgery is done for Graves' orbitopathy (thyroid eye disease). Reference summaries put clinically obvious eye disease in roughly 20 to 25 percent of people with Graves' hyperthyroidism and severe disease in about 3 to 5 percent; women are affected about four times as often as men, and smoking is a major risk factor.[10][27][1] Earlier epidemiological reviews describe two incidence peaks, in the fifth and seventh decades of life.[27]

The condition is autoimmune: antibodies directed at thyroid-stimulating hormone receptors in orbital tissue are associated with muscle enlargement, fat expansion and swelling, and because the bony orbit cannot expand, pressure rises and the eye is pushed forward.[10][28] Disease passes through an active inflammatory phase and a more stable, fibrotic phase. Guidelines recommend managing the active phase with risk-factor control, selenium in some settings, intravenous glucocorticoids and other immunosuppression, with rehabilitative surgery delayed until the disease has been stable, normally for at least six months.[1][25][10]

Rehabilitative surgery is usually performed in a sequence that reflects function: decompression to reduce proptosis, then squint surgery for double vision, then eyelid surgery. Eyelid retraction procedures are the most commonly performed operation and can lower the upper lid by several millimetres.[10] A review of dysthyroid optic neuropathy notes that decompression with two or three walls improves visual function in people with compressed optic nerves, and that evidence on the best sequence of steroids versus surgery is limited.[5]

Targeted medicines have changed the field. Teprotumumab, which blocks the IGF-1 receptor, was approved by the US FDA in January 2020 for thyroid eye disease and is discussed in reviews as an alternative route to reduce proptosis without surgery in some patients.[10][3] A registered phase 2 trial planned to start in 2026 compares a teprotumumab product with methylprednisolone after urgent decompression for dysthyroid optic neuropathy.[32]

Decompression removes bone from one or more orbital walls, with or without orbital fat removal, to let tissue expand. Approaches include endoscopic transnasal (reported in 1990),[12] transantral (a 1993 series of 428 patients),[13] transcaruncular,[14] and transconjunctival or transnasal endoscopic comparisons.[7] A 2006 paper described transpalpebral orbital lipectomy as an alternative.[11]
Surgery for thyroid eye disease is typically delayed until disease has been stable for at least six months unless the optic nerve is threatened.[10]

Variants described in the literature differ in what is removed and from where. Medial wall and floor removal, often through the nose or sinus (endoscopic transnasal or transantral), gives room into the ethmoid and maxillary sinuses; lateral wall decompression, sometimes with rim-sparing designs, gives room into the temporal fossa; fat-only decompression removes orbital fat without bone; and balanced or customised multi-wall approaches combine them according to the patient's anatomy.[12][13][17][16] Registered trials include a comparison of two decompression techniques in 42 patients with Graves orbitopathy and a study of a treatment for temporal hollowing, a recognised cosmetic after-effect of lateral wall work.[30][31]

Forum discussions often distinguish surgeons who 'shave bone' from those who 'remove fat', and treat the choice as determining how much posterior movement is achievable.[18] Clinicians in the published series tie technique choice to the amount of proptosis, orbital anatomy and disease phase rather than to a fixed rule.[7][13]

A 2025 randomised trial of 48 moderate-to-severe or sight-threatening orbits compared transconjunctival and transnasal endoscopic decompression, with effectiveness defined by postoperative proptosis or proptosis reduction.[7] A randomised trial of rehabilitative decompression in Graves' orbitopathy and another combining decompression with intraoperative muscle relaxation for esotropia have also been published.[8][9]

The 1993 series of 428 patients treated by the transantral route is among the largest reported and is widely cited in later work, as is the 1990 report of the endoscopic transnasal route.[13][12] More recent randomised trials compare approaches, with outcomes defined by postoperative proptosis, proptosis reduction, and in one trial the resolution of esotropia.[7][8] A randomised trial of rehabilitative decompression for Graves' orbitopathy examined functional and appearance results after the operation.[9]

Endocrinology reviews note that surgery is among the options that can address fibrotic or fat-expanded orbits that no longer respond to anti-inflammatory therapy, because inflammation can quickly leave irreversible fibrosis and increased orbital fat behind.[29][26]

Reported complications in thyroid eye disease include optic neuropathy, corneal exposure, persistent double vision and raised intraocular pressure.[10] A case report describes vision loss and recurrent proptosis after an uncomplicated fat-only decompression.[6] Persistent diplopia and new strabismus are recognised outcomes in the literature, and orbital compartment syndrome is described as an ophthalmic surgical emergency.[15]

Beyond the complications above, temporal hollowing after lateral wall decompression, new or worsened double vision, numbness of the cheek, sinus problems after medial or floor work, and the need for further eyelid or squint surgery are all reported in the thyroid literature.[10][31][15] Guidelines recommend that decompression be done by surgeons experienced in orbital surgery.[1][25]
A forum reply to a thread on the topic cites a 9.3% complication rate and calls it one of the riskiest hardmaxxing procedures.[19]

Clinical studies involve patients with thyroid eye disease: randomised trials of surgical approach,[7][8][9] registered trials of customised multi-wall decompression and rim-sparing lateral wall techniques,[16][17] and case series.[13] No study was found of orbital decompression for cosmetic deep-setting of eyes in people without thyroid disease.

Threads ask how to tell if cosmetic orbital decompression is needed, who qualifies, whether it is superior to other eye surgeries, and the difference between surgeons who remove fat and those who shave bone.[18][21][22][23][24] Some repliers recommend orbital fat grafting as an alternative for people who do not have markedly protruding eyes, and others discuss a fear of botched outcomes.[19] Members also post personal accounts of surgery with a named surgeon.[20]

Posters ask how to avoid being 'botched' or blind, and weigh decompression against alternatives such as orbital fat grafting, under-eye support (filler or implants) and weight loss that alters fat pads around the eye.[19][35] A thread titled around destroying the bilateral orbital decompression pill shows that the value of operating on both eyes is itself debated.[34] Another asks about decompression for asymmetric eyes, where the question is whether to operate on one side or both.[36]

The community vocabulary is mostly descriptive of the look: 'bug eyes' or 'protruding eyes' for a prominent globe, 'deep set' for an eye placed well back under the brow ridge, and 'hunter eyes' for a related ideal. Candidates are generally imagined to be people whose eyes sit forward of the cheek and brow when seen from the side; threads ask how that is measured.[24][21]

timeline.event: Robert Graves describes the link between thyroid enlargement and eye protrusion.[10]
A JAMA editorial of the period describes Graves' eye protrusion mechanisms as well understood, a statement later reviewers cite as an example of shifting theories about the disease.[26]
Endoscopic transnasal orbital decompression is described.[12]
A series of 428 transantral decompressions for severe Graves' ophthalmopathy is reported.[13]
The transcaruncular approach to the medial orbit and orbital apex is described.[14]
Transpalpebral orbital lipectomy is described as an alternative route to reduce orbital fat.[11]
The European Thyroid Association and EUGOGO publish management guidelines for Graves' orbitopathy.[25]
Teprotumumab is approved by the US FDA for thyroid eye disease.[10]
EUGOGO publishes updated medical management guidelines for Graves' orbitopathy.[1]
A randomised trial compares transconjunctival and transnasal approaches to endoscopic decompression.[7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org orbital decompression is regarded as one of the most aggressive eye hardmaxxing options, and threads compare candidacy, technique and botch risk.[18][19][21][22]

claims.claim: Orbital decompression is the way to get deep-set eyes if yours protrude.
claims.believers: Posters ask whether it is the only way to fix protruding eyes and whether it is superior to other eye surgeries.[22][23]
claims.experts: Established indications are thyroid eye disease and compressive optic neuropathy; no cosmetic-indication trials were found.[1][9]

claims.claim: Only people with genuinely bulging eyes are candidates; others should use fat grafts instead.
claims.believers: A reply states that it is for people with 'genuine bug eyes' and suggests orbital fat grafts for others.[19]
claims.experts: The literature defines proptosis thresholds in thyroid eye disease trials (for example postoperative proptosis under 18 mm as one outcome criterion), not cosmetic candidacy.[7]

claims.claim: The surgery is high-risk and can cause botched or sight-threatening outcomes.
claims.believers: Posters cite a 9.3% complication rate and a fear of blindness or asymmetry.[19]
claims.experts: Reviews and case reports describe optic neuropathy, diplopia and vision loss after decompression in thyroid eye disease.[6][10]

claims.claim: Surgeons differ on whether to remove fat or bone, and this changes results.
claims.believers: One thread notes some surgeons remove fat while others shave bone.[18]
claims.experts: Trials compare approaches in thyroid eye disease; outcomes depend on technique and disease severity.[7][13]

claims.claim: Orbital decompression produces the deep-set 'hunter eye' look in people with normal eyes.
claims.believers: Posters describe it as the way to move the globe back when the eye sits forward of the brow and cheek, and post experiences with named surgeons.[20][35]
claims.experts: Published results concern people with thyroid eye disease, where reduction in proptosis is the outcome measured; no trial has tested it in people with normal orbital status.[7][9]

claims.claim: Fat grafting or under-eye support is a safer substitute for decompression.
claims.believers: A reply recommends orbital fat grafts for people who do not have markedly protruding eyes.[19]
claims.experts: Transpalpebral lipectomy and fat removal are described in the thyroid literature as ways to reduce orbital volume; grafting for cosmetic eye support is not covered by the trials located here.[11]

claims.claim: Surgeon choice and technique decide the outcome.
claims.believers: Threads stress seeking surgeons with experience and distinguishing fat-only from bone work.[18][20]
claims.experts: Guidelines recommend that surgery be done by experienced orbital teams after disease is stable, and case reports note vision loss after even uncomplicated fat-only surgery.[1][6]

claims.claim: Weight loss or low body fat can make eyes look more protruding, adding to the case for surgery.
claims.believers: A poster on looksmax.org argues that losing facial fat can reduce under-eye support and make bulging eyes more noticeable.[35]
claims.experts: No published study located examines facial fat loss and apparent globe position in people without thyroid disease.

card.summary: Orbital bone or fat removal that lets the eye sit deeper; a thyroid-eye-disease operation with no trials for cosmetic deep-setting.
card.aka: Cosmetic orbital decompression, deep-set eye surgery
card.note: Orbital surgery with risks to vision and eye movement; evidence comes from thyroid eye disease, not cosmetic use.

quick.overview:
Orbital decompression enlarges the eye socket by removing bone, fat or both so the eye sits further back. It is an established operation for thyroid eye disease, where swollen tissue pushes the eyes forward or threatens the optic nerve.

Looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a way to get deeper-set eyes without thyroid disease and debate candidacy and technique. No published trial studies it for that cosmetic purpose.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons remove parts of orbital walls (medial, lateral, floor) and/or orbital fat via endoscopic, conjunctival or other approaches, giving swollen or prominent contents room to move backward.
quick.risks: Reported complications in thyroid eye disease include optic neuropathy, corneal exposure, persistent double vision and raised eye pressure, and vision loss after decompression has been described in case reports. Forum posters call it among the riskiest hardmaxxing procedures.
